articles.title: Labels are texts too

body.support:
A food packet is a text. It talks to **two kinds of reader**.

The **front** is for shoppers walking past. It is bright. It wants to sell.

The **back** is there to tell you facts.

1. **Health stars.** Half a star up to 5. More stars is healthier. Only compare foods that are alike.
2. **Ingredients.** The list goes from the most to the least.
3. **Nutrition panel.** A table of what is inside. Use the **per 100 g** column to compare.
4. **Allergens.** Look for the word **“Contains”**.
5. **Dates.** **Use-by** is about safety. **Best-before** is about how good it tastes.

You don't read a label from top to bottom. You **scan** for the part you need.
body.core:
A food packet is a text with **two audiences**. The front is for the shopper walking past: bright colours, a big name and **claims** like “high in fibre”. Its job is to sell. The back and sides are there to inform, and the law says certain facts must be there.

1. **Health Star Rating.** From half a star up to five. More stars means a healthier choice, but only compare **similar** foods, like cereal with cereal.
2. **Ingredients.** Listed from the **most to the least**. If sugar is near the start, there's a lot of it.
3. **Nutrition panel.** A table of what's inside, per serve and **per 100 g**. Use per 100 g to compare two products fairly, because serve sizes are different.
4. **Allergens.** Foods like peanuts, milk, egg and wheat must be shown. Many packs have a **“Contains:”** line.
5. **Dates.** A **use-by** date is about safety: don't eat it after that day. A **best-before** date is about quality: it may still be fine after.

You don't read a label from top to bottom. You **scan** it: decide what you need, go straight to that part, and check.
body.extend:
A food packet is a text written for **two audiences** with two purposes. The front targets a shopper who will glance at it for a second or two: colour, branding and **claims** such as “high in fibre” are designed to persuade. The back and sides inform, and food standards law requires certain information to be there.

1. **Health Star Rating.** A rating from half a star to five that summarises the overall nutrition of a packaged food. It's only useful when comparing **similar** products.
2. **Ingredients.** Listed in order of weight, from most to least, so the first few tell you what you're mostly eating.
3. **Nutrition information panel.** Average amounts per serve and **per 100 g**. Serve sizes vary between brands, so per 100 g is the fair comparison.
4. **Allergens.** Common allergens such as peanuts, milk, egg and wheat must be declared, often in a **“Contains:”** statement.
5. **Dates.** A **use-by** date is a safety limit; a **best-before** date is a quality guide.

Skilled readers don't read labels in order. They **scan** with a purpose: decide what they need, locate the right section, and check the detail.

caseStudies.title: The Health Star Rating

body.support:
Food labels can be hard to read fast. So the government made a shortcut. It is called the **Health Star Rating**. It started in **2014**.

It goes from **half a star to 5 stars**. More stars means a healthier choice.

The rule: only compare foods that are **alike**. A cereal with a cereal. Not a cereal with a yoghurt.

It is **voluntary**. That means companies can choose not to use it. So some packets don't have stars.
body.core:
Food labels can be hard to read in a hurry. So the Australian, state and territory and New Zealand governments built a shortcut: the **Health Star Rating**. It started in **June 2014**.

The rating goes from **half a star to five stars**. It's worked out from what's in 100 g or 100 mL of the food: things like energy, saturated fat, sugar and sodium, and also fibre, protein, and fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes.

The official advice is to compare **similar** foods, found in the same part of the supermarket. Compare a cereal with a cereal, not a cereal with a yoghurt.

It has limits. The system is **voluntary**, so not every product shows it. And it doesn't count everything, like vitamins or how the food was made.
body.extend:
Nutrition panels are dense, and shoppers make decisions in seconds. To bridge that gap, the Australian, state and territory and New Zealand governments introduced the **Health Star Rating** system in **June 2014**.

The rating runs from **half a star to five stars** and is calculated per 100 g or 100 mL. It weighs energy, saturated fat, sugar and sodium against positive components such as fibre, protein, and fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes.

The official guidance is to use it only to compare **similar** products from the same part of the supermarket.

The system has limits. It is **voluntary**, so many products don't display it, and it doesn't account for everything, such as vitamins and minerals or how a food is processed. It's a shortcut, not the whole story.

teacher.overview: Students learn that a food label is an everyday text with two audiences and purposes (the front sells, the back informs), name its features, scan it for key information and decode tricky label words. The hands-on task has them compare two real packets and justify a choice with evidence. The case study is the government's Health Star Rating system.
prep: Collect empty packets (cereal boxes, drink bottles, snack bars, yoghurt tubs). Ask students to bring two of the same kind from home.
Optional: plan a short walk to a local supermarket, or set the label hunt as homework.
Have the Health Star Rating “For shoppers” page ready to show.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Front sells, back tells
steps: **Hook (10 min):** hold up two cereals. Vote: which is healthier? Reveal the backs.
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** the parts of a label and their jobs; model scanning with a think-aloud.
**Read (15 min):** Labels are texts too + questions.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Scan it, crack it
steps: **Race the label (10 min):** timed scanning questions; discuss strategies.
**Decoding (15 min):** model breaking up “unsweetened”; students do Crack the word in pairs.
**Case study (15 min):** the Health Star Rating.
**Set up (10 min):** explain the label hunt; check everyone has two packets.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Choose and prove it
steps: **Hands-on (25 min):** label hunt table and Do it page with real packets.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Label:** 1 claim (front); 2 Health Star Rating; 3 ingredients (most to least); 4 nutrition panel (per serve and per 100 g); 5 allergens; 6 best-before date (quality).

**Race the label:** 24 g of sugar per 100 g; sugar is the second ingredient, so there's a lot of it; no — it contains wheat (allergen line).

**Crack the word (sample):** un + sweet + ened = no sugar added to sweeten it; saturate(d) = full of / soaked (a type of fat); carbo + hydrate = carbohydrates (sugars and starches); preserve + ative = something added to make food last longer.
